# Percentage Change

{{< include _common.qmd >}}

We compare changes in percentage terms all the time. A \$1 price
increase means something very different for a \$4 coffee than for a \$4,000
laptop. Percentage changes put both on the same scale, and are the
building block of **elasticity**.

## The method

When a value changes from an original value $x_0$ to a new value $x_1$:

$$
\%\Delta x = \frac{x_1 - x_0}{x_0} \times 100
$$

Take the change, divide by the **starting** value, and multiply by
100. Increases are positive and decreases are negative.

::: {.callout-note}
## Example
A price rises from \$10 to \$12. The change is \$2, so the percentage change is
$$
\frac{12 - 10}{10} \times 100 = \frac{2}{10} \times 100 = 20\%.
$$
:::

## Percentage changes don't always reverse nicely

Suppose the price then falls back from \$12 to \$10. The change is −\$2, but the
starting value is now \$12:

$$
\frac{10 - 12}{12} \times 100 = -16.67\%
$$

A 20% increase followed by a 16.67% decrease gets you back where you started.
The same \$2 is a smaller share of a bigger base. To fix this we can use
the *midpoint formula* (a.k.a. *arc elasticity*), which divides by the average of the two values so that
the answer is the same in both directions.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistakes
- Dividing by the new value instead of the starting value.
- Forgetting to multiply by 100 if you want a percentage measure: 0.2 is the change as a decimal; 20% is the
  percentage.
- Dropping the minus sign on a decrease.
:::
